tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. For all other deposits: (a) Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement, if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. Your objection must be sent to (landlord’s address) . If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant. (b) Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages. The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action. (c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. The court shall advance the cause on the calendar. (d) Compliance with this section by an individual or business entity authorized to conduct business in this state, including Florida-licensed real estate brokers and sales associates, constitutes compliance with all other relevant Florida Statutes pertaining to security deposits held pursuant to a rental agreement or other landlord-tenant relationship. Enforcement personnel shall look solely to this section to determine compliance. This section prevails over any conflicting provisions in chapter 475 and in other sections of the Florida Statutes, and shall operate to permit licensed real estate brokers to disburse security deposits and deposit money without having to comply with the notice and settlement procedures contained in s. 475.25 (1)(d). (4) This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs including s. 202, s. 221(d)(3) and (4), s. 236, or s. 8 of the National Housing Act, as amended, other than for rent stabilization. With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes. (5) Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year, must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached. Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it. (6) For the purposes of this part, a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement, and any security deposit carried forward shall be considered a new security deposit. (7) Upon the sale or transfer of title of the rental property from one owner to another, or upon a change in the designated rental agent, any and all security deposits or advance rents being held for the benefit of the tenants shall be transferred to the new owner or agent, together with any earned interest and with an accurate accounting showing the amounts to be credited to each tenant account. Upon the transfer of such funds and records to the new owner or agent, and upon transmittal of a written receipt therefor, the transferor is free from the obligation imposed in subsection (1) to hold such moneys on behalf of the tenant. answer:
To answer your questions:

### What You Can Do
You can object in writing to the landlord's $400 claim for carpet replacement:

1. **Send a written objection by September 8, 2026.** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(b), you have 15 days after receiving the landlord's notice to object to the claim or the amount. Because you received the letter on August 24, 2026, your 15-day deadline to object is September 8, 2026, which has not passed. In your objection, you can state that the carpet condition was due to normal wear and use rather than damage. Section 6 of your lease requires you only to "leave the apartment clean and empty" at move-out and does not establish any carpet replacement fee.
2. **Deliver the objection properly.** Section 7 of your lease provides that written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." 
3. **If you do not object within 15 days**, Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(b) authorizes the landlord to deduct the $400 claim from your deposit. However, that subsection also specifies that "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action."
4. **Dispute resolution and attorney's fees.** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(c), if either you or the landlord files a court action over the right to the security deposit, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney."

### When You Get the Other $650
Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(b), the landlord "shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." 

Because the landlord's notice was dated August 20, 2026, the landlord must send you the remaining $650 by September 19, 2026, which has not passed.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the landlord has not returned the tenant's security deposit and has not sent a written claim against it. It rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If the tenant says the landlord sent anything in writing about keeping part of the deposit (a letter, an e-mail, a text, a portal message), also load deposit_claim_received. Whether that notice came in time, and the tenant's 15 days to object, belong there.
- Money the lease labels nonrefundable may fall under 83.491 instead. Do not treat it as outside 83.49 without reading 83.491 (fetch it with get_statute_section).
- The statute names deposits it does not cover: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(4)).
- Whether the tenant's college housing is outside part II altogether has not been checked for this situation. Section 83.42 lists what part II does not apply to, among them "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). Fetch 83.42 with get_statute_section and read it before telling the tenant either way.
- The tool does not decide whether any exclusion applies. Say what the words are and what you would need to know.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- The security deposit clause: the amount, and that the lease calls it a deposit.
- Any money labeled nonrefundable (see 83.491 above).
- What the lease says about the tenant's forwarding address. The landlord's notice goes to the tenant's "last known mailing address".
- The move-out requirements. Cleaning and carpet clauses are the usual basis of a claim.
- Where and how the tenant's notices to the landlord must be sent.
- Any term on notice before the tenant moves out early (see the 7-day notice below).
- Whether one roommate's damage can be charged against the whole deposit.
- The date the lease term ends.

### From the tenant

- How much was the deposit? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- What date did the lease end, or what date was it terminated? Put it beside the lease's end date, and tell the tenant when they differ.
- What date did they move out and return the keys?
- Have they received anything in writing from the landlord about keeping part of the deposit (a letter, an e-mail, a text, a portal message)? If so, what date did it reach them, and how: certified mail, regular mail, e-mail, handed to them, a text or a resident portal message, something else, or they do not know?
- Did they give the landlord their new mailing address in writing?
- Did they move out before the lease end date, or was this a month-to-month arrangement?
- If so, have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out, and how did it reach the landlord: handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the rental agreement ended. The landlord's 15 days and 30 days count from it. When it differs from the move-out date, the program records the move-out date beside it (see the first open question below).
- The date the tenant moved out. The tenant's 7 days' notice counts back from it.
- Whether the tenant moved out before the lease's end, or has a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy. The 7-day notice counts only then.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- Proof the deposit was paid.
- The move-out date: a key receipt, a walkthrough form, the last utility bill.
- Move-in and move-out photos.
- The forwarding-address notice, with proof of delivery.
- Any landlord letters or e-mails, with the envelope or the full headers.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do this and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below).

### Get the whole deposit back because the landlord gave no notice of a claim within the 30 days (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a))

All three conditions must be met. This situation lists no steps beyond a letter asking for the deposit (see Letters).

1. The landlord gave the tenant no written notice of a claim on the deposit. The statute: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). The tenant can tell you:
   - Nothing in writing about keeping part of the deposit arrived: met.
   - Something arrived by certified mail: not met here. Whether it came in time belongs to deposit_claim_received.
   - Something arrived another way (regular mail, e-mail, handed over, a text or portal message, something else): whether a notice given that way is the required notice is not settled. The statute names two ways: "by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). See the second open question.
   - The tenant does not know how it came: ask them to check the envelope (a certified mail label or receipt) or the e-mail, which shows it.
2. The 30 days after the end of the rental agreement have passed: "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show the 30 days have not passed, a notice of a claim may still come in time, so the option is not open yet.
3. The landlord was not relieved of that notice. The statute relieves the landlord when a tenant who leaves early, or has a periodic tenancy, gives no 7 days' notice: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). This is met in any of these ways:
   - The tenant did not move out before the lease's end, and the tenancy was not month to month or another periodic one. The tenant can tell you.
   - The tenant gave the landlord 7 days' written notice, by certified mail or in person, with an address: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Ask the tenant to check that the notice reached the landlord at least 7 days before they moved out (the program's deadlines show the last day) and gave the address where they can be reached.
   - The tenant e-mailed that notice, which counts only as 83.505 allows. They check whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and the same two points as above. Also read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord with search_lease and say what it says.
   - The notice went some other way (regular mail, a portal message, a text, something else). They check how it reached the landlord, beside the two ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.
   - The lease provides otherwise on notice before moving out, and the tenant followed it: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Read the lease's clause on notice before moving out with search_lease, say what it says, and ask whether the tenant followed it.

Which date counts as the end of the rental agreement is also open (the first open question below).

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation.

- The landlord's 15 days to return the deposit when no claim is intended. It counts from the date the rental agreement ended. The statute: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- The landlord's 30 days to give written notice of a claim. It counts from the same date. The notice must go by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address, or by e-mail as 83.505 allows: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). If it is missed: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before moving out. It counts back from the date the tenant moved out, and only when the tenant moved out before the lease's end or has a periodic tenancy. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (quoted above under the third condition). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise ("Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement", Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)); read its clause on notice before moving out.

## What the statute does not settle

For each of these, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading and what it would mean for them, and pick none.

### Which date is the termination of the rental agreement

The 15-day and 30-day clocks run from "termination of the rental agreement". The text does not say whether that is the lease end date or the move-out date when the two differ; when they are the same day the question does not arise. The program counts from the date the tenant confirmed as the end of the lease and records the move-out date beside it.

- The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. And 83.49(5) speaks of a tenant who "vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so leaving early does not by itself end the agreement.
- The move-out date: the disclosure 83.49(2)(d) requires tells the tenant that the landlord must give notice "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(2)(d)), which reads the same clock as running from the day the tenant leaves.

### A notice of a claim that came some way other than certified mail

The statute names two ways to give the notice of a claim (quoted under the first condition). 83.505(1) allows e-mail only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)). Apply these to how the tenant says the notice came. If the tenant has not said whether they signed such an addendum, that condition is not known yet. What stays open is a notice that reached the tenant in time some other way.

- A notice given another way is not the required written notice, and "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- A notice the tenant actually received in time is enough: 83.505(6) says the section "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law" (Fla. Stat. 83.505(6)), and the tenant had what the notice is for.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the obligation identified, the amount and the return address, a response deadline computed by the tool, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States move-out date, amount, forwarding address. Asks for return. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(3)(a) obligation, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the forfeiture consequence, quoted, and 83.49(3)(c) fee-shifting.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that sending it does not start any deadline the program computes for this situation. The only notice from a tenant that the program tracks here is the one in 83.49(5), which says that "any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)) "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The same sentence also covers week-to-week, month-to-month, and other periodic tenancies. Whether it applies to them turns on when they moved out and on their lease (the sentence begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement", Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)); offer to apply it to their confirmed facts.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Applying either landlord clock without saying which date it counts from, or using the lease end date without the move-out date beside it.
- Saying the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim unless the record shows both conditions: the tenant confirmed that no notice of a claim arrived, and the program's deadlines list the 30-day notice date as passed. Never your own count.
- Stopping at the forfeiture. The same sentence lets the landlord "file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- Applying 83.49(3)(a) to an early move-out or a periodic tenancy without 83.49(5), whose missing 7-day notice "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).
- Promising fees and costs without the condition in 83.49(3)(c), which applies when "either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(c)), and then to the prevailing party.
- Treating a nonrefundable fee as outside 83.49 without reading 83.491.
- Computing any date yourself.

The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . No, you cannot demand all of it yet on the ground that the landlord missed a deadline. 

Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a), whether the landlord must return the deposit within 15 days depends on whether they intend to make a claim:
- "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement."
- "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim."

Both periods count from the termination of the rental agreement, which matches your move-out date of July 31, 2026. Counting from that date:
- The 15-day period ended on August 15, 2026, which has passed.
- The 30-day period ends on August 30, 2026, which has not passed.

Because the 30-day window has not expired, the landlord still has time to send a written notice of intent to impose a claim. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a), the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim against the deposit only "[i]f the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period." Until August 30, 2026 passes without that notice, a demand claiming the landlord has forfeited the deposit is premature. Even after a forfeiture, the statute provides that the landlord "may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant."

Note also that under Fla. Stat. § 83.42(1), this chapter does not apply to residency in a facility "when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." Whether off-campus college housing falls under this exclusion depends on how closely the housing is tied to the educational institution.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the landlord has not returned the tenant's security deposit and has not sent a written claim against it. It rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If the tenant says the landlord sent anything in writing about keeping part of the deposit (a letter, an e-mail, a text, a portal message), also load deposit_claim_received. Whether that notice came in time, and the tenant's 15 days to object, belong there.
- Money the lease labels nonrefundable may fall under 83.491 instead. Do not treat it as outside 83.49 without reading 83.491 (fetch it with get_statute_section).
- The statute names deposits it does not cover: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(4)).
- Whether the tenant's college housing is outside part II altogether has not been checked for this situation. Section 83.42 lists what part II does not apply to, among them "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). Fetch 83.42 with get_statute_section and read it before telling the tenant either way.
- The tool does not decide whether any exclusion applies. Say what the words are and what you would need to know.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- The security deposit clause: the amount, and that the lease calls it a deposit.
- Any money labeled nonrefundable (see 83.491 above).
- What the lease says about the tenant's forwarding address. The landlord's notice goes to the tenant's "last known mailing address".
- The move-out requirements. Cleaning and carpet clauses are the usual basis of a claim.
- Where and how the tenant's notices to the landlord must be sent.
- Any term on notice before the tenant moves out early (see the 7-day notice below).
- Whether one roommate's damage can be charged against the whole deposit.
- The date the lease term ends.

### From the tenant

- How much was the deposit? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- What date did the lease end, or what date was it terminated? Put it beside the lease's end date, and tell the tenant when they differ.
- What date did they move out and return the keys?
- Have they received anything in writing from the landlord about keeping part of the deposit (a letter, an e-mail, a text, a portal message)? If so, what date did it reach them, and how: certified mail, regular mail, e-mail, handed to them, a text or a resident portal message, something else, or they do not know?
- Did they give the landlord their new mailing address in writing?
- Did they move out before the lease end date, or was this a month-to-month arrangement?
- If so, have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out, and how did it reach the landlord: handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the rental agreement ended. The landlord's 15 days and 30 days count from it. When it differs from the move-out date, the program records the move-out date beside it (see the first open question below).
- The date the tenant moved out. The tenant's 7 days' notice counts back from it.
- Whether the tenant moved out before the lease's end, or has a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy. The 7-day notice counts only then.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- Proof the deposit was paid.
- The move-out date: a key receipt, a walkthrough form, the last utility bill.
- Move-in and move-out photos.
- The forwarding-address notice, with proof of delivery.
- Any landlord letters or e-mails, with the envelope or the full headers.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do this and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below).

### Get the whole deposit back because the landlord gave no notice of a claim within the 30 days (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a))

All three conditions must be met. This situation lists no steps beyond a letter asking for the deposit (see Letters).

1. The landlord gave the tenant no written notice of a claim on the deposit. The statute: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). The tenant can tell you:
   - Nothing in writing about keeping part of the deposit arrived: met.
   - Something arrived by certified mail: not met here. Whether it came in time belongs to deposit_claim_received.
   - Something arrived another way (regular mail, e-mail, handed over, a text or portal message, something else): whether a notice given that way is the required notice is not settled. The statute names two ways: "by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). See the second open question.
   - The tenant does not know how it came: ask them to check the envelope (a certified mail label or receipt) or the e-mail, which shows it.
2. The 30 days after the end of the rental agreement have passed: "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show the 30 days have not passed, a notice of a claim may still come in time, so the option is not open yet.
3. The landlord was not relieved of that notice. The statute relieves the landlord when a tenant who leaves early, or has a periodic tenancy, gives no 7 days' notice: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). This is met in any of these ways:
   - The tenant did not move out before the lease's end, and the tenancy was not month to month or another periodic one. The tenant can tell you.
   - The tenant gave the landlord 7 days' written notice, by certified mail or in person, with an address: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Ask the tenant to check that the notice reached the landlord at least 7 days before they moved out (the program's deadlines show the last day) and gave the address where they can be reached.
   - The tenant e-mailed that notice, which counts only as 83.505 allows. They check whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and the same two points as above. Also read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord with search_lease and say what it says.
   - The notice went some other way (regular mail, a portal message, a text, something else). They check how it reached the landlord, beside the two ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.
   - The lease provides otherwise on notice before moving out, and the tenant followed it: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Read the lease's clause on notice before moving out with search_lease, say what it says, and ask whether the tenant followed it.

Which date counts as the end of the rental agreement is also open (the first open question below).

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation.

- The landlord's 15 days to return the deposit when no claim is intended. It counts from the date the rental agreement ended. The statute: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- The landlord's 30 days to give written notice of a claim. It counts from the same date. The notice must go by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address, or by e-mail as 83.505 allows: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). If it is missed: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before moving out. It counts back from the date the tenant moved out, and only when the tenant moved out before the lease's end or has a periodic tenancy. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (quoted above under the third condition). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise ("Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement", Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)); read its clause on notice before moving out.

## What the statute does not settle

For each of these, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading and what it would mean for them, and pick none.

### Which date is the termination of the rental agreement

The 15-day and 30-day clocks run from "termination of the rental agreement". The text does not say whether that is the lease end date or the move-out date when the two differ; when they are the same day the question does not arise. The program counts from the date the tenant confirmed as the end of the lease and records the move-out date beside it.

- The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. And 83.49(5) speaks of a tenant who "vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so leaving early does not by itself end the agreement.
- The move-out date: the disclosure 83.49(2)(d) requires tells the tenant that the landlord must give notice "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(2)(d)), which reads the same clock as running from the day the tenant leaves.

### A notice of a claim that came some way other than certified mail

The statute names two ways to give the notice of a claim (quoted under the first condition). 83.505(1) allows e-mail only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)). Apply these to how the tenant says the notice came. If the tenant has not said whether they signed such an addendum, that condition is not known yet. What stays open is a notice that reached the tenant in time some other way.

- A notice given another way is not the required written notice, and "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- A notice the tenant actually received in time is enough: 83.505(6) says the section "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law" (Fla. Stat. 83.505(6)), and the tenant had what the notice is for.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the obligation identified, the amount and the return address, a response deadline computed by the tool, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States move-out date, amount, forwarding address. Asks for return. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(3)(a) obligation, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the forfeiture consequence, quoted, and 83.49(3)(c) fee-shifting.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that sending it does not start any deadline the program computes for this situation. The only notice from a tenant that the program tracks here is the one in 83.49(5), which says that "any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)) "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The same sentence also covers week-to-week, month-to-month, and other periodic tenancies. Whether it applies to them turns on when they moved out and on their lease (the sentence begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement", Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)); offer to apply it to their confirmed facts.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Applying either landlord clock without saying which date it counts from, or using the lease end date without the move-out date beside it.
- Saying the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim unless the record shows both conditions: the tenant confirmed that no notice of a claim arrived, and the program's deadlines list the 30-day notice date as passed. Never your own count.
- Stopping at the forfeiture. The same sentence lets the landlord "file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- Applying 83.49(3)(a) to an early move-out or a periodic tenancy without 83.49(5), whose missing 7-day notice "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).
- Promising fees and costs without the condition in 83.49(3)(c), which applies when "either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(c)), and then to the prevailing party.
- Treating a nonrefundable fee as outside 83.49 without reading 83.491.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. answer:
No, your landlord does not automatically have to return your entire deposit simply because they never sent you a notice of claim. 

Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who intends to claim deductions against a security deposit must give written notice by certified mail (or permitted e-mail) within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord fails to send that notice within the 30-day period, the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim on the deposit (though the landlord may still file a lawsuit for damages after returning the deposit). 

Whether "termination of the rental agreement" means your move-out date or your lease end date is not settled by Florida law:
- One reading is that it means the move-out date, because the statutory disclosure in Fla. Stat. § 83.49(2)(d) states that notice must be given "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT". Thirty days from your move-out date of June 15, 2026 was July 15, 2026, which has passed.
- The other reading is that it means the lease end date, because Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a) refers to "vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" as separate concepts, and Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5) treats vacating before the expiration of the term as occurring prior to termination. Thirty days from your lease end date of July 31, 2026 was August 30, 2026, which has also passed.

However, because you moved out on June 15, 2026—before your lease ended on July 31, 2026—Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5) applies. Under that subsection, a tenant who leaves early must give "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached," unless the written lease provides otherwise. 

Your lease does not provide an exception. Section 6 provides that you must "give Landlord a forwarding address in writing," Section 7 requires written notices to Landlord to be "delivered by hand to the office... or sent there by certified mail," and Section 8 states that you and the landlord "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail." A text message without a forwarding address does not satisfy Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5).

Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5), failing to give that 7 days' notice "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)". Because your landlord was relieved of the duty to send a 30-day claim notice, they did not forfeit their right to make deductions simply by not sending one.

Even so, Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5) specifies that your failure to give that notice "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." You can still request the return of your $1,050 deposit, but the landlord is allowed to dispute your refund and claim legitimate charges, such as unpaid rent or physical damage to Apartment 12.

Finally, Fla. Stat. § 83.42(1) excludes housing from Florida's residential landlord-tenant act when residency is "incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." If Lakeview Terrace Apartments is private, off-campus housing, chapter 83 applies; if it were a university-operated facility where residence is incidental to educational services, these statutory rules would not govern.

Did you pay rent for July 2026 through the end of your lease term?

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the landlord has not returned the tenant's security deposit and has not sent a written claim against it. It rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If the tenant says the landlord sent anything in writing about keeping part of the deposit (a letter, an e-mail, a text, a portal message), also load deposit_claim_received. Whether that notice came in time, and the tenant's 15 days to object, belong there.
- Money the lease labels nonrefundable may fall under 83.491 instead. Do not treat it as outside 83.49 without reading 83.491 (fetch it with get_statute_section).
- The statute names deposits it does not cover: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(4)).
- Whether the tenant's college housing is outside part II altogether has not been checked for this situation. Section 83.42 lists what part II does not apply to, among them "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). Fetch 83.42 with get_statute_section and read it before telling the tenant either way.
- The tool does not decide whether any exclusion applies. Say what the words are and what you would need to know.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- The security deposit clause: the amount, and that the lease calls it a deposit.
- Any money labeled nonrefundable (see 83.491 above).
- What the lease says about the tenant's forwarding address. The landlord's notice goes to the tenant's "last known mailing address".
- The move-out requirements. Cleaning and carpet clauses are the usual basis of a claim.
- Where and how the tenant's notices to the landlord must be sent.
- Any term on notice before the tenant moves out early (see the 7-day notice below).
- Whether one roommate's damage can be charged against the whole deposit.
- The date the lease term ends.

### From the tenant

- How much was the deposit? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- What date did the lease end, or what date was it terminated? Put it beside the lease's end date, and tell the tenant when they differ.
- What date did they move out and return the keys?
- Have they received anything in writing from the landlord about keeping part of the deposit (a letter, an e-mail, a text, a portal message)? If so, what date did it reach them, and how: certified mail, regular mail, e-mail, handed to them, a text or a resident portal message, something else, or they do not know?
- Did they give the landlord their new mailing address in writing?
- Did they move out before the lease end date, or was this a month-to-month arrangement?
- If so, have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out, and how did it reach the landlord: handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the rental agreement ended. The landlord's 15 days and 30 days count from it. When it differs from the move-out date, the program records the move-out date beside it (see the first open question below).
- The date the tenant moved out. The tenant's 7 days' notice counts back from it.
- Whether the tenant moved out before the lease's end, or has a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy. The 7-day notice counts only then.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- Proof the deposit was paid.
- The move-out date: a key receipt, a walkthrough form, the last utility bill.
- Move-in and move-out photos.
- The forwarding-address notice, with proof of delivery.
- Any landlord letters or e-mails, with the envelope or the full headers.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do this and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below).

### Get the whole deposit back because the landlord gave no notice of a claim within the 30 days (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a))

All three conditions must be met. This situation lists no steps beyond a letter asking for the deposit (see Letters).

1. The landlord gave the tenant no written notice of a claim on the deposit. The statute: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). The tenant can tell you:
   - Nothing in writing about keeping part of the deposit arrived: met.
   - Something arrived by certified mail: not met here. Whether it came in time belongs to deposit_claim_received.
   - Something arrived another way (regular mail, e-mail, handed over, a text or portal message, something else): whether a notice given that way is the required notice is not settled. The statute names two ways: "by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). See the second open question.
   - The tenant does not know how it came: ask them to check the envelope (a certified mail label or receipt) or the e-mail, which shows it.
2. The 30 days after the end of the rental agreement have passed: "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show the 30 days have not passed, a notice of a claim may still come in time, so the option is not open yet.
3. The landlord was not relieved of that notice. The statute relieves the landlord when a tenant who leaves early, or has a periodic tenancy, gives no 7 days' notice: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). This is met in any of these ways:
   - The tenant did not move out before the lease's end, and the tenancy was not month to month or another periodic one. The tenant can tell you.
   - The tenant gave the landlord 7 days' written notice, by certified mail or in person, with an address: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Ask the tenant to check that the notice reached the landlord at least 7 days before they moved out (the program's deadlines show the last day) and gave the address where they can be reached.
   - The tenant e-mailed that notice, which counts only as 83.505 allows. They check whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and the same two points as above. Also read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord with search_lease and say what it says.
   - The notice went some other way (regular mail, a portal message, a text, something else). They check how it reached the landlord, beside the two ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.
   - The lease provides otherwise on notice before moving out, and the tenant followed it: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Read the lease's clause on notice before moving out with search_lease, say what it says, and ask whether the tenant followed it.

Which date counts as the end of the rental agreement is also open (the first open question below).

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation.

- The landlord's 15 days to return the deposit when no claim is intended. It counts from the date the rental agreement ended. The statute: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- The landlord's 30 days to give written notice of a claim. It counts from the same date. The notice must go by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address, or by e-mail as 83.505 allows: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). If it is missed: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before moving out. It counts back from the date the tenant moved out, and only when the tenant moved out before the lease's end or has a periodic tenancy. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (quoted above under the third condition). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise ("Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement", Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)); read its clause on notice before moving out.

## What the statute does not settle

For each of these, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading and what it would mean for them, and pick none.

### Which date is the termination of the rental agreement

The 15-day and 30-day clocks run from "termination of the rental agreement". The text does not say whether that is the lease end date or the move-out date when the two differ; when they are the same day the question does not arise. The program counts from the date the tenant confirmed as the end of the lease and records the move-out date beside it.

- The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. And 83.49(5) speaks of a tenant who "vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so leaving early does not by itself end the agreement.
- The move-out date: the disclosure 83.49(2)(d) requires tells the tenant that the landlord must give notice "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(2)(d)), which reads the same clock as running from the day the tenant leaves.

### A notice of a claim that came some way other than certified mail

The statute names two ways to give the notice of a claim (quoted under the first condition). 83.505(1) allows e-mail only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)). Apply these to how the tenant says the notice came. If the tenant has not said whether they signed such an addendum, that condition is not known yet. What stays open is a notice that reached the tenant in time some other way.

- A notice given another way is not the required written notice, and "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- A notice the tenant actually received in time is enough: 83.505(6) says the section "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law" (Fla. Stat. 83.505(6)), and the tenant had what the notice is for.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the obligation identified, the amount and the return address, a response deadline computed by the tool, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States move-out date, amount, forwarding address. Asks for return. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(3)(a) obligation, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the forfeiture consequence, quoted, and 83.49(3)(c) fee-shifting.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that sending it does not start any deadline the program computes for this situation. The only notice from a tenant that the program tracks here is the one in 83.49(5), which says that "any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)) "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The same sentence also covers week-to-week, month-to-month, and other periodic tenancies. Whether it applies to them turns on when they moved out and on their lease (the sentence begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement", Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)); offer to apply it to their confirmed facts.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Applying either landlord clock without saying which date it counts from, or using the lease end date without the move-out date beside it.
- Saying the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim unless the record shows both conditions: the tenant confirmed that no notice of a claim arrived, and the program's deadlines list the 30-day notice date as passed. Never your own count.
- Stopping at the forfeiture. The same sentence lets the landlord "file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)).
- Applying 83.49(3)(a) to an early move-out or a periodic tenancy without 83.49(5), whose missing 7-day notice "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).
- Promising fees and costs without the condition in 83.49(3)(c), which applies when "either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(c)), and then to the prevailing party.
- Treating a nonrefundable fee as outside 83.49 without reading 83.491.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. answer:
Whether the landlord can keep the $400 turns on whether a text message satisfies Florida’s notice requirement. As for the remaining $650, the landlord cannot keep it, because even under the landlord’s own text, no claim was made against that portion.

### The $400 Claim
Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a), if a landlord intends to impose a claim on a security deposit, they must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice "by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim," and the notice must include statutory language warning the tenant of their 15-day deadline to object. 

Both your confirmed lease end date (2026-07-31) and your confirmed move-out date (2026-07-31) were July 31, 2026. The 30-day deadline passed on August 30, 2026. 

Section 8 of your lease specifies that "Landlord and Tenant have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail." You received only a text message on August 18, 2026, and nothing by certified mail or e-mail. 

The law is unsettled on whether actual receipt of a notice by another method (such as a text message) counts:
- **One reading:** The text is not the required notice. Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a) explicitly mandates notice "by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505", containing specific statutory wording. Under this reading, because the landlord failed to provide the required statutory notice within 30 days, the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a)). If so, they cannot keep the $400 from the deposit.
- **The other reading:** The text gave you actual notice of the claim within the 30-day window, and Fla. Stat. § 83.505(6) provides that the electronic notice statute "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." Under this reading, if a court were to treat the text as sufficient notice, the landlord could seek to retain the $400 for actual damage, though they would still have to prove the carpet replacement was legitimate damage beyond normal wear and tear.

### The Remaining $650
Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a), if the landlord does not intend to claim against the deposit, they must return it "within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement." That 15-day deadline passed on August 15, 2026. 

Even if the text were treated as an intended claim on part of the deposit, Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(b) requires the landlord to "remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." Under either provision, the landlord has no right to hold the $650 and must return it to you.

### Exclusions
Under Fla. Stat. § 83.42(1), chapter 83 does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." If Lakeview Terrace Apartments is standard private off-campus housing, chapter 83 applies; if it is direct university-operated housing where residence is incidental to educational services, chapter 83 may not apply. Additionally, Fla. Stat. § 83.49(4) excludes housing where the rent or deposit is regulated by a public body.

If you send a demand letter to the landlord, Section 7 of your lease requires:
"Written notices to Landlord shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail."
